ch06.f.d.mode: Increase a horizontal pull steadily, or tilt the board steadily
ch06.f.d.mat: Materials of block and surface: they set the static coefficient $\mu_s$ and the kinetic coefficient $\mu_k$
ch06.f.d.m: Block mass $m$: $mg$, $N$ and the friction scale with $m$
ch06.f.goal.static: Static friction: only as large as needed, at most $\mu_s N$
ch06.f.goal.kinetic: When the block starts to slide, friction drops to $\mu_k N$ ($\mu_k < \mu_s$) and stays there
ch06.f.obs.match: At rest: the $f$ curve lies on the pull $F$ (dashed), $f_s = F$
ch06.f.obs.drop: When $f$ reaches $\mu_s N$ the block starts to slide, $f$ drops to $\mu_k N$ and $v$ starts to grow
ch06.f.obs.angle: Tilting board: sliding starts at the angle with $\tan\theta_c = \mu_s$ (wood 26.6°, ice 5.7°). A different mass scales $mg$, $N$ and $f$ with $m$, while $\theta_c$ and the sliding acceleration $a = g(\sin\theta_c - \mu_k\cos\theta_c)$ do not depend on it
ch06.f.obs.mat: On the incline $N = mg\cos\theta$, so $\mu_s N$ shrinks as the angle grows
ch06.f.assume: The pull grows at 2 N/s per kg of block (4 N/s at 2 kg), so every force scales with $m$ while the slip time, acceleration and speed do not depend on it. The board tilts at 6°/s and is held at the angle where sliding starts; typical friction coefficients. Force arrows are proportional to the force at one mass; across masses their length changes only gently (about 1.5 times from 0.5 to 10 kg) to stay on the stage
ch06.c.d.preset: Four situations in which different real forces keep the object on the circle
ch06.c.d.cut: The string breaks after a quarter turn
ch06.c.d.ice: The car reaches ice after a quarter turn ($\mu_s = 0.1$)
ch06.c.goal.net: Uniform circular motion: the net force points to the centre and has size $mv^2/r$
ch06.c.goal.notnew: Centripetal force = the radial component of the net force. It is not a new kind of force; tension, friction or a normal force plays that role
ch06.c.obs.flat: Flat curve: static friction $f_s$ is the centripetal force. Maximum static friction $f_{s,\text{max}} = \mu_s mg$ → highest speed without skidding $\sqrt{\mu_s g r}$. On ice ($\mu_s = 0.1$) a faster car skids off along the tangent
ch06.c.obs.cut: Cut string, or a skid on the icy road: once the inward force is gone the object moves straight along the tangent; without an inward net force there is no circular motion. The cut conical pendulum also falls under gravity alone (side view; its tangential motion is perpendicular to the view)
ch06.c.goal.rot: Non-inertial frame (rotating with the object): the object rests → real forces + centrifugal force $F_\text{cf}$ = 0
ch06.c.obs.rot: Non-inertial (rotating) view: the object stays put while the ground marks turn the other way (clockwise). An outward centrifugal force $F_\text{cf} = mv^2/r$ (dashed) balances the real forces, so $\sum F'_r = 0$. The centrifugal force is a fictitious (inertial) force: no object exerts it
ch06.c.assume: Ball on a string: 0.5 kg, radius 1 m, frictionless table. Curves: 1000 kg, radius 20 m. Flat curve: dry road $\mu_s = 0.6$ (no skid over the speed range), ice $\mu_s = 0.1$, friction neglected once skidding. Banked curve: 20°, dry road (no skid over the range). Conical pendulum: 1 m string. The top views share one drawn radius; top-view arrows use one fixed scale per situation (set at its top speed), side-view force arrows are scaled relative to $mg$. Non-inertial (rotating) frame: it coincides with the inertial frame at $t = 0$ and turns at $\omega = v/r$. The side view shows only the centrifugal force, which is radial; the Coriolis force, whose direction turns in the horizontal plane, is shown in the top view only
ch06.c.d.v: Speed $v$ around the circle (range depends on the situation). The conical pendulum keeps a 1 m string; its angle follows from $v$
ch06.c.d.rot: Adds a panel in the non-inertial frame turning with the object: the object rests, the centrifugal force (dashed) balances the real forces. After the cut or the skid also the Coriolis force
ch06.c.obs.v: Doubling $v$ makes the needed net force $mv^2/r$ four times larger. Arrow lengths use one fixed scale per situation
ch06.c.obs.bank: Banked curve: at the design speed $v_\text{d} = \sqrt{g r\tan\theta}$ no friction is needed and $N\sin\theta$ is the centripetal force. $v > v_\text{d}$ → $f_s$ points down the slope ($f_s > 0$ in Σ), $v < v_\text{d}$ → up the slope ($f_s < 0$). The dashed $f_s\cos\theta$ in the side view is the horizontal component of the friction
ch06.c.obs.cone: Conical pendulum: the horizontal component $T\sin\theta$ of the tension is the centripetal force; the vertical component balances $mg$. Fixed string length $L$, $r = L\sin\theta$, $\tan\theta = v^2/(g r)$ → the faster it goes, the more the string tilts
